A wind turbine, a bridge, a jet engine. Imagine each had a living copy inside a computer, obeying the same physics.
That copy is a digital twin: a virtual model of one specific physical thing, linked to it by data throughout its life. It has three parts: the object, the model, and the connection.
If data moves by hand, it is only a digital model. If data flows automatically from object to model, it is a digital shadow. It becomes a twin when information also flows back and acts on the object.
So how is that different from a simulation? A simulation is an experiment you run and close. A twin persists, with one identity and one history, checked against reality again and again.

Even before anything is built, the twin can work. Its first data are the laws of nature: gravity, the stiffness of steel, the conservation of energy. A solver steps these equations through time, so engineers can ask: what if the load doubles?

Now the lifecycle. Phase zero: the prototype twin designs the product. Phase one: the digital thread builds it. Phase two: the instance twin runs it with live sensors. Phase three: the aggregate twin learns from the fleet. Phase four: it retires, and its lessons shape the next design.
Physics gives the twin its first life. Data keeps it honest. Now explore it for yourself.
